# Beyond IPF: Pulmonary Function Test Predictors of Echocardiographic Pulmonary Hypertension Across the Spectrum of ILD

**Authors:** Julia K Munchel; Bess M Flashner; Ryosuke Imai; Cyrus A Kholdani; Rene S Bermea; Anjali Singh; Robert W Hallowell; Mary B Rice; Andrew J Synn

**Affiliations:** 1 Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care, and Sleep Medicine, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2 Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Department of Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3 Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Thoracic Center, St. Luke's International Hospital, St Luke's International University, Tokyo, Japan

## Abstract

Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a common complication of interstitial lung disease (ILD), yet data on screening in heterogenous ILD populations are limited. We evaluated whether routinely measured pulmonary function test (PFT) parameters identify individuals with intermediate‐to‐high echocardiographic risk of PH. 432 ILD patients met inclusion criteria with an echocardiogram reporting peak tricuspid regurgitant velocity (TRV) and a PFT reporting diffusion impairment (DLCO) within 1 year (median interval, 39 days). Of these, 126 underwent right heart catheterization (RHC). Age‐ and sex‐ adjusted logistic regression assessed associations between %predicted forced vital capacity (FVC), %predicted DLCO, and FVC/DLCO ratio with intermediate‐to‐high echocardiographic PH probability (TRV > 2.8 m/s). Receiver operating characteristic curves evaluated diagnostic performance. The cohort included 28% systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease‐associated ILD, 27% interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features, and 6% idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, with a mean age of 72% and 54% female. Lower FVC and DLCO were associated with higher odds of echocardiographic PH (OR 1.35, 95%CI 1.21–1.50; OR 1.50, 95%CI 1.36–1.73) and increases in FVC/DLCO ratio similarly predicted risk (OR 1.83, 95%CI 1.44–2.32). DLCO had the highest predictive ability (AUC 0.74, 95%CI 0.69–0.79) with an optimal cut‐off of 42% (sensitivity 67%, specificity 74%). In patients who underwent RHC, TRV > 2.8 m/s correlated with mean pulmonary artery pressure (r = 0.55, 95%CI 0.42–0.66) and tripled the odds of confirmed PH (OR 3.75, 95%CI 2.25–6.24). In sum, severe diffusion impairment, regardless of fibrosis extent, may detect patients with ILD who warrant echocardiographic screening, specialty PH referral, and consideration of RHC.

Keywords: FVC/DLCO ratio, Group III PH, interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features, screening

Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a common and clinically significant complication of interstitial lung disease (ILD) with a pooled prevalence of 37%–40% [1]. Patients with interstitial lung disease‐associated pulmonary hypertension (ILD‐PH) have worse outcomes compared to those without, with a greater need for supplemental oxygen, decreased exercise tolerance, more frequent acute exacerbations, and higher mortality [2]. Despite the 2021 FDA approval of inhaled treprostinil, the first therapy for ILD‐PH shown to improve 6‐min walk distance and possibly survival, there remain no formal guidelines for systematic PH screening in ILD [3, 4].

The 2022 European Society of Cardiology/European Respiratory Society (ESC/ERS) guidelines recommend an echocardiographic assessment of PH probability to inform referral to specialty centers and the need for invasive evaluation with right heart catheterization (RHC), but these recommendations do not address screening in ILD specifically [5]. Additionally, although echocardiography has a high positive predictive value, it still results in a small number of RHCs in patients without PH and a significant minority of ILD patients with PH are misclassified as “low probability” using these guidelines in isolation [6]. Studies suggest that the diagnostic accuracy of echocardiographic measures is strengthened when combined with pulmonary function test (PFT) parameters, mirroring approaches successfully applied in systemic sclerosis‐associated pulmonary hypertension (SSc‐PH), where algorithms such as DETECT and ASIG have improved detection when compared to the ESC/ERS guidelines, in part by capitalizing on the predictive value of the % predicted forced vital capacity (FVC)/% predicted diffusion capacity (DLCO) ratio [7, 8, 9, 10]. The ASIG algorithm, in particular, may be applicable to an ILD cohort, and not merely to patients with systemic sclerosis, considering it is a simple, two‐step screening tool that utilizes readily available and routinely acquired clinical information (N‐terminal pro‐B type natriuretic peptide and FVC/DLCO ratio as first‐tier tests followed by echocardiography) [7, 11].

Efforts to translate similar tools to ILD‐PH more broadly have yielded mixed results [12]. Prior studies, focused on smaller cohorts of homogenous patient populations, most commonly in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and fibrotic lung disease, have reported inconsistent findings on the predictive value of the FVC/DLCO ratio [12, 13, 14, 15]. Most recently, the FORD score (FVC/DLCO ratio, Oxygen saturation nadir during 6‐min walk test, Race, and Distance) incorporated this parameter but was again limited to an IPF cohort [14]. Our goal was to determine how our ILD population, especially in a landscape of ever increasing patient phenotyping, aligns with the ESC/ERS diagnostic algorithm. We hypothesized that in a large and diverse ILD cohort, routinely measured PFT parameters could identify individuals at an intermediate‐to‐high echocardiographic risk of PH and, therefore, identify those in whom further invasive work‐up with RHC or referral to a PH center for specialized care is indicated.

## Methods

This study was approved by the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Massachusetts General Hospital Institutional Review Boards. Patients were retrospectively identified from a database of patients with ILD of any cause who were evaluated at two academic medical centers in Boston that serve as PH and ILD referral centers. As described in prior publications, patients were identified for inclusion in the database if they had an available serologic work‐up (particularly if positive for Mi‐2, NXP‐2, or MDA5) or if they were designated by their treating pulmonologist as a patient with ILD appropriate for inclusion [16, 17, 18]. The underlying ILD etiology was determined by the patient's treating pulmonologist and then confirmed by study investigators. Interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features (IPAF) diagnoses were adjudicated by a pulmonologist at the time of entry into the database according to the 2015 ERS/ATS research classification criteria [19]. Eligible patients had an outpatient echocardiogram (TTE) that reported a peak tricuspid regurgitant velocity (TRV) and a PFT that reported a DLCO measured within 1 year (Figure 1). When a patient had multiple TTEs, PFTs, or RHCs documented, those tests performed the closest together were selected for analysis. Consequently, although the majority of PFTs (58%) preceded the TTE which preceded the RHC (78%), this was not required for inclusion.

*Figure 1: Study flow diagram.*

Statistical analyses were performed using RStudio version 2025.05.1 Build 513. Multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for age and sex were used to determine if PFT parameters (% predicted FVC, % predicted DLCO [corrected for hemoglobin if available], and FVC/DLCO ratio) were associated with an intermediate‐to‐high probability of pulmonary hypertension as defined by a peak TRV > 2.8 m/s. Although no single echocardiographic parameter can reliably establish PH, the 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines recommend using peak TRV rather than estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure due to inaccuracies in estimating right atrial pressure [5]. Tricuspid regurgitation gradient has also been validated as a screening tool for incident PH in a mixed population [20]. In our institutions, as in other studies, application of the full algorithm recommended in the guidelines is challenging because many echocardiographic signs of PH in addition to TRV are not routinely documented [6]. Therefore, we selected the cut‐off of > 2.8 m/s without accounting for the presence of these other signs of PH on echocardiogram or risk factors associated with pulmonary hypertension because use of this cut off alone identifies patients who warrant referral to a specialized PH center for comprehensive evaluation and invasive assessment when appropriate.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were generated and area under the curves (AUC) were calculated to assess the overall diagnostic performance of PFT parameters in predicting an echocardiographic peak TRV > 2.8 m/s. Optimal cut‐off values were then determined by selecting the point that maximized the Youden Index, which represents the threshold that provides the best balance between sensitivity and specificity.

Lastly, in the subset of patients that underwent RHC, patients were included for analysis regardless of their underlying hemodynamic subtype. Multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for age and sex were used to determine the association between peak TRV > 2.8 m/s on TTE and a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) of > 20 mmHg on RHC.

## Results

432 out of 1046 patients in the database met inclusion criteria (Figure 1). The mean age was 72 ± 11 years old, 54% were female, and 55% were ever smokers. 28% had systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease‐associated interstitial lung disease (SARD‐ILD), 27% met IPAF criteria, and a minority of patients had an idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (IIP), including 6% with IPF. The median interval between PFT and TTE was 39 days (IQR 12‐84); in the 126 patients who also underwent RHC, the median interval between TTE and RHC was 42 days (IQR 11‐120). Elevated TRV > 2.8 m/s was observed in 39% of patients. Lung function demonstrated moderate restriction (mean % predicted FVC 76 ± 21) and moderate diffusion impairment (mean % predicted DLCO 52 ± 21). The median FVC/DLCO ratio was 1.48 (IQR 1.2‐1.9) (Table 1).

In the multivariable logistic regression models controlling for age and sex, per 10% lower predicted FVC and predicted DLCO were each associated with greater odds of an intermediate‐to‐high echocardiographic probability of PH (OR 1.35, 95% CI[1.21–1.50] and OR 1.50, 95% CI[1.36–1.73] respectively) (Figure 2). Similarly, per standard deviation higher FVC/DLCO ratio was also associated with greater odds of an intermediate‐to‐high echocardiographic probability of PH (OR 1.83, 95% CI[1.44–2.32]) (Figure 2). Notably, when % predicted DLCO was included in the % predicted FVC model, the association between FVC and echocardiographic PH was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (OR 1.12, 95%CI[0.98–1.27]).

*Figure 2: Comparison of the associations between PFT parameters (FVC, DLCO, FVC/DLCO ratio) and odds of intermediate‐to‐high echocardiographic probability of PH in the entire ILD cohort (OR with 95% CI error bars). CI= confidence interval, DLCO= % predicted diffusion capacity of carbon monoxide, FVC= % predicted forced vital capacity, ILD= interstitial lung disease, OR= odds ratio, PFT= pulmonary function test, PH= pulmonary hypertension.*

Compared to % FVC or FVC/DLCO ratio, % predicted DLCO had the best ability to predict an intermediate‐to‐high echocardiographic probability of PH with an AUC of 0.74 (95% CI 0.69–0.79) and a suggested optimal cut‐off of 42% (95% CI 41–44%) with a sensitivity of 67% and a specificity of 74% The diagnostic performance of % predicted FVC and FVC/DLCO ratio were inferior predictors for intermediate‐to‐high echocardiographic probability of PH and our data suggested an optimal screening cut‐off for FVC/DLCO ratio of 1.4, but with poor sensitivity and specificity (AUC 0.69, 95%CI[0.64–0.74] and AUC 0.69, 95% CI[0.63–0.74] respectively) (Figure 3).

*Figure 3: ROC curves for prediction of intermediate‐to‐high probability of echocardiographic PH by FVC (A), DLCO (B), and FVC/DLCO ratio (C). DLCO= % predicted diffusion capacity of carbon monoxide; FVC= % predicted forced vital capacity; PH= pulmonary hypertension; ROC=receiver operating characteristic.*

In our group of patients who also underwent RHC, 67% had pre‐capillary PH, 24% had combined pre‐ and post‐capillary PH, and 8% had isolated post‐capillary PH. Hemodynamic classification could not be determined in 3 patients because of missing data. In this group as a whole, peak TRV positively correlated with mPAP and patients with a peak TRV > 2.8 m/s had over three times higher odds of having invasively confirmed PH independent of age and sex (r = 0.55, 95% CI[0.42–0.66] and OR 3.75, 95%CI[2.25–6.24]) (Figure 4 and eTable 1).

*Figure 4: Scatter plot showing association between peak TRV and mPAP in the entire ILD cohort. ILD= interstitial lung disease; mPAP= mean pulmonary artery pressure; TRV= tricuspid regurgitant velocity.*

Results and demographics were consistent across institutions and after excluding patients with SSc. In subgroup analyses (IPAF, SARD‐ILD, IIP, and FEV1/FVC < 0.7), the SARD‐ILD group was younger, more often female, and had fewer ever smokers (eTable 2–5). Despite these differences, the proportion of patients with invasively diagnosed PH and the associations between peak TRV and PFT parameters were similar across groups (Figure 5).

## Discussion

In this large and diverse ILD cohort, PFT parameters (% predicted FVC, % predicted DLCO, and FVC/DLCO ratio) were each associated with higher odds of intermediate‐to‐high probability of PH on TTE. Patients meeting this echocardiographic threshold had more than a threefold increase in odds of having invasively confirmed PH. Importantly, when DLCO was added to the FVC model, the association between FVC and echocardiographic PH became non‐significant. In diagnostic performance analyses, % predicted FVC and the FVC/DLCO ratio were less accurate than % predicted DLCO alone, for which an optimal screening cut‐off of 42% was identified.

These findings support the long‐standing recommendation that PH should be suspected when DLCO is significantly reduced, and a threshold of 40% has previously been proposed as clinically meaningful [12, 21]. Our results extend this observation by showing that patients with ILD and a severely reduced DLCO should be screened for PH regardless of clinical, radiographic, or PFT assessment of fibrosis severity. Both the FVC/DLCO ratio AUC curve and the multivariable model controlling for DLCO indicate that the apparent association between FVC and echocardiographic PH is largely mediated by impaired gas exchange, and that incorporating FVC may dilute the predictive accuracy of DLCO despite its theoretical role in accounting for restrictive physiology. In our cohort, % predicted DLCO alone provided greater discriminatory ability than the multifactorial prediction model described by Nathan et al. for IPF, which combined FVC/DLCO ratio, oxygen desaturation nadir, race, and 6‐min walk distance [14]. Although the FVC/DLCO ratio cutoff we identified (1.4) is consistent with prior reports, its poor specificity and sensitivity make it unsuitable for PH screening across all‐cause ILD [21]. One possible explanation for this discrepancy between our results and prior work highlighting the utility of the FVC/DLCO ratio may be that our cohort included patients earlier in their disease course, with less pronounced FVC reduction and milder PH. This is supported by the relatively low median mPAP of 31 mmHg in those with RHC‐confirmed PH compared to the higher values reported in other RHC cohorts [22, 23]. If so, this would be clinically advantageous, as identifying patients earlier in their disease trajectory offers greater opportunity for timely intervention.

Overall, our results are consistent in both direction and magnitude with previous studies in more narrowly defined populations such as IPF, fibrotic ILD, and SSc‐ILD [12, 21]. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate the ability of PFT parameters to identify PH across a heterogeneous ILD cohort, including in patients with IPAF. Based on our results, screening strategies informed by PFTs appear broadly applicable to all patients with ILD, without the need for tailoring by underlying diagnosis or additional risk stratification in concomitant PH‐associated conditions such as SSc. The unique composition of our cohort may also explain some of the differences between our findings and prior reports highlighted above.

This study has several strengths, including its large sample size, diverse patient population, and inclusion of data from two ILD referral centers. Nonetheless, there are limitations. As with any retrospective study, selection bias is possible based on which patients underwent TTE and RHC as well as based on which patients performed a DLCO. Patients without a recorded DLCO could represent individuals with more advanced lung disease who were unable to perform the maneuver. However, at our institutions, a DLCO is not routinely obtained with every PFT, and we are unable to distinguish retrospectively whether the absence of a DLCO reflected an inability to perform the test or simply that it was not ordered. Importantly, only a small proportion of otherwise eligible patients (3%) were excluded for this reason. Such biases may limit generalizability, although our findings are largely concordant with prior studies and remained consistent across subgroup analyses. Another limitation is the temporal gap between testing: although some patients underwent PFT, TTE, and RHC on the same day, the median interval was 39‐42 days. Given the known variability in mPAP, with spontaneous fluctuations of up to 22% within just a few hours, this may have contributed to imperfect correlation across modalities [24]. Finally, our reliance on TRV alone to define echocardiographic probability of PH may have underestimated disease burden, since patients with PH but low TRV would be misclassified [6].

These limitations underscore the persistent challenge of PH screening in ILD. Without systematic RHC, the number of missed diagnoses remains unknown, particularly among patients with low TRV or in those lacking additional echocardiographic markers. Future strategies should consider incorporating more readily available alternative or complementary echocardiographic measures that particularly correlate closely with invasive hemodynamics in low‐TRV patients. Similarly, although the carbon monoxide transfer coefficient was not available in our dataset, it is a commonly measured PFT parameter that may provide complementary physiological information beyond % predicted DLCO and warrants further investigation. Ultimately, integrating PFT parameters (most notably % predicted DLCO) with echocardiographic indices and imaging markers such as pulmonary artery diameter or the pulmonary artery‐to‐aorta ratio may provide a more robust screening framework and more readily identify patients who would benefit from initiation of therapy.

In conclusion, our findings support systematic screening for PH in ILD patients with severe diffusion impairment, independent of fibrosis extent. Casting a wide net for screening is increasingly critical now that effective therapies are available which can improve quality of life and potentially survival [3, 4].
